newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Nestle says optimistic about 1996. [CORRECTED 16:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Nestle says optimistic about 1996. [CORRECTED 16:00 GMT]

text.p: Nestle on Wednesday said it was optimistic for 1996, forecasting that net profit would be above three billion Swiss francs ($2.4 billion), thanks in part to favourable currency exchange rates.
The company said that for the first time in a few years, exchange rates had a beneficial impact on Nestle's results.
The Swiss franc's recent declines have been positive for export-dependent firms based in Switzerland.

"Unless there is a very volatile turn-around in the currency market, we can expect net profits to grow faster than sales. In absolute terms they will certainly exceed three billion (francs)," Nestle chairman Helmut Maucher told journalists gathered at the company's headquarters for presentation of its 10-month results.
"We are expecting to finish the year with turnover of close to 60 billion ($47.4 billion) unless unexpectedly volatile currency fluctuations take place in the meantime," he said.
His forecast compared with consolidated net profits in 1995 of 2.92 billion francs ($2.3 billion), and sales of 56.48 billion ($44.58 billion).
Maucher said he was optimistic about growth continuing in the coming years, but provided no figures.
"I am an optimist as to continued growth in trade and net consolidated profit for next year as well as for the years to come," Maucher said.

Sales appeared to be turning higher in the second half of 1996, with October sales (corrects from "10-month sales") up 12 percent versus October 1995. But he said sales so far have not developed in a "completely satisfying" manner.

Nestle said its sales for the first 10 months of 1996 grew 5.7 percent versus the comparable 1995 period, to 48.3 billion Swiss francs ($38.1 billion) from 45.7 billion ($36.1 billion) in the 1995 10 months.
Sales volume growth in January to October was three percent, a slight slowing from the 3.6 percent reported for the first half.

"This slight slowdown of growth is largely due to bad weather conditions in Europe in August and September, which naturally had a negative impact on sales of mineral water and ice cream," Nestle said.
Wilhelm Blaeuer, analyst at Geneva-based Pictet & Cie Bank said ice cream sales were probably a major factor dampening growth.
"Its (Nestle's) earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) generated from ice cream is mainly European-biased, despite the fact they are trying to expand," Blaeuer said.
He also expected Nestle to lower prices, if it hadn't already, to boost coffee and ground coffee sales in the United States and Japan. He continued to rate Nestle as a "hold" in a model portfolio.
